qt: to the Commission Kim Van Sparrentak (Verts/ALE), Mohammed Chahim (S&D) Subject:

According to reports, there are many illegal vape advertisements on Snapchat driving children into the arms of predatory, non-licensed vape dealers on a large scale1. Dutch doctors have raised this pressing issue. At the same time, an increasing number of children are in hospital with severe medical problems caused by vaping, such as lung punctures, brain damage or heavy metals in their bodies2. 1.

Is the Commission investigating Snapchat for spreading illegal content, which is a violation of the Digital Services Act (DSA)3, including the provisions on notice and action4 and on systemic risks to health and safety and protection of minors5?

Will the Commission consider EU-wide action to ensure that vapes become less attractive to children, less poisonous and less dangerous, such as by banning flavoured vapes, introducing neutral packaging and increasing safety standards, for instance by introducing a ban on poisonous heavy metals from vapes in the anticipated review of the Tobacco Products Directive6?

Is the Commission considering an EU-wide ban on single-use disposable vapes, given their devastating environment impact and potential violation of the EU rules on waste from electrical and electronic equipment, following the examples of Belgium, France and Spain and recent discussions in the Netherlands?

at: (English version) to the Commission Kim Van Sparrentak (Verts/ALE), Mohammed Chahim (S&D) (2 September 2025) Subject: Prohibited predatory marketing of illicit vapes to children on Snapchat and severe medical harm to children caused by vapes According to reports, there are many illegal vape advertisements on Snapchat driving children into the arms of predatory, nonlicensed vape dealers on a large scale (1). Dutch doctors have raised this pressing issue. At the same time, an increasing number of children are in hospital with severe medical problems caused by vaping, such as lung punctures, brain damage or heavy metals in their bodies (2). 1. Is the Commission investigating Snapchat for spreading illegal content, which is a violation of the Digital Services Act (DSA) (3), including the provisions on notice and action (4) and on systemic risks to health and safety and protection of minors (5)? 2. Will the Commission consider EU-wide action to ensure that vapes become less attractive to children, less poisonous and less dangerous, such as by banning flavoured vapes, introducing neutral packaging and increasing safety standards, for instance by introducing a ban on poisonous heavy metals from vapes in the anticipated review of the Tobacco Products Directive (6)? 3. Is the Commission considering an EU-wide ban on single-use disposable vapes, given their devastating environment impact and potential violation of the EU rules on waste from electrical and electronic equipment, following the examples of Belgium, France and Spain and recent discussions in the Netherlands? (20 October 2025) The Commission is aware of reports concerning the dissemination of illegal advertisements of drugs, alcohol and nicotinerelated products to minors on Snapchat. Under the Digital Services Act (1), Snapchat was designated by the Commission as a very large online platform and is subject to a set of reinforced obligations. The provider of Snapchat is required to diligently identify, assess and analyse the systemic risks stemming from the design, functioning and use made of its services and related systems and put in place effective measures to mitigate the identified systemic risks. All providers of online platforms accessible to minors, are required to ensure a high level of privacy, safety and security to minors. The Commission is working closely with the Dutch Digital Services Coordinator, Autoriteit Consument en Markt, who is currently investigating Snapchat’s compliance with these obligations (2). The Commission is evaluating the Tobacco Products Directive (3) and Tobacco Advertising Directive (4). The evaluation is looking at young people’s access to novel tobacco and nicotine products and the findings will inform the next steps concerning these two Directives.

Obligations for the collection of e-cigarettes are covered by the waste electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE) Directive (5). WEEE collection points must be provided to enable users to discard e-cigarettes and return used e-cigarettes free of charge when buying new ones. The Batteries Regulation (6) requires that portable batteries incorporated in products marketed in the EU are readily removable and replaceable at any time during the lifetime of the product. This provision will ban e-cigarettes that do not have readily removable and replaceable batteries.
